title: Persuasion and Skin in the Game
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Argues that advocates become far more persuasive when they demonstrably live by the same terms they're asking others to accept -- the classic 'skin in the game' principle. Contrasts words, which are cheap, with shared experience and shared consequences, which signal that an advocate's belief is tested rather than performed. The practical challenge posed to leaders and organizations is whether they use their own products, services, and advice internally, since visibly practicing what's preached lowers resistance and converts claims into commitments.
points: Advocacy becomes far more persuasive when the advocate visibly lives under the same constraints and risks as the audience being persuaded.
Shared consequences -- time, money, reputation -- are what separate tested belief from a sales pitch in the eyes of a skeptical audience.
The practical test for any organization is whether its own leaders and team members use the products, services, or advice they promote to others.
quotes: Believing in the advice, products, recommendations, or services others advocate for is much easier when the other party practices what they preach.
Advocates for just about anything are more convincing when they can prove they have “skin in the game.” And the skin that matters most is shared experience.
When someone lives within the same constraints, accepts the same tradeoffs, and faces the same risks, their message carries a different weight. It no longer feels self-interested. It feels tested.
Take a hard look at what you, your team, or your organization sells, promotes, and advocates for. Does everyone in the organization eat their own cooking?
Everyone knows that words are inexpensive and engagement is costly.
Matching deeds to declarations lays the groundwork for persuasion. Without living the proof, advocacy is just another sales job.
